This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

#8821. 14-Minute Seated Yoga to Help You Unwind Before Bed

Shaunneka Hewitt is the founder of the YouTube channel Move with Shaunneka and has more than a decade of yoga teaching experience. Her approach is rooted in the belief that movement should feel good and allow you to slow down and listen to your body, which is exactly the aim of this seated yoga practice before bed.

Maybe you’re not one to curate the “perfect” nighttime routine. After all, what even is that? Your typical evening might consist of working until you can barely keep your eyes open or doomscrolling in bed until you essentially pass out mid-swipe. But technically, you already have a nighttime routine, whether it’s intentional or not. So you might as well make it work for you.

That doesn’t mean your pre-sleep schedule needs to include Himalayan-salt-lamp lighting and bubble baths. It can be much simpler. When you steal just a few minutes from the end of your day for checking in with yourself, as opposed to checking out, you give your entire body a break from the busy day. Practicing even a few minutes of seated yoga before bed is one way to reintroduce your body to the idea of rest after a long day of, well, not resting.

These stretches are inspired by the longer holds of yin yoga, and if you have the time, by all means, linger in each shape for 3 to 5 minutes. There’s no Savasana, with the hope that your final resting pose happens in the comfort of your bed as you drift off to sleep.

Sit on the mat and draw the soles of your feet together, letting your knees lower to the sides. Reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling, then hinge forward with a flat back so your chest is over your legs in Butterfly Pose (Bound Angle Pose). For more of a stretch, use your elbows to gently press your thighs away from you. Breathe here, then slowly return to an upright position.

From Butterfly legs, keep your left leg bent and straighten your right leg to the side with your toes pointed toward the ceiling. Slowly fold forward straight ahead, lowering your fingertips or forearms to the mat in a variation of Half Butterfly Pose. Relax your neck and let your head hang as you breathe here, then slowly roll up to an upright position.

From Half Butterfly legs, shift your weight into your left leg as you bend your right knee behind you at about a 90-degree angle and draw the sole of your right foot toward your right glute. Draw the sole of your left foot toward your right knee in Deer Pose (also known as 90/90). Inhale and twist toward your right; exhale and lower your fingertips or forearms to the floor outside your right thigh in Deer Pose Twist. Breathe here, then slowly roll up.

From Deer Pose, press your hands or fingertips into the mat to frame your left leg and draw your left foot closer toward your hips. Straighten your right leg behind you in Pigeon Pose. Inhale and reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling; exhale and fold forward over your left leg, resting your hands or forearms on the mat. Breathe here.

Repeat Butterfly Pose, Half Butterfly Pose, Deer Pose Twist, and Pigeon Pose on the opposite side.

Sit on the mat with your legs extended in a wide V shape and your toes pointed toward the ceiling. Press your heels into the mat. Inhale and reach the crown of your head toward the ceiling; exhale and fold forward, lowering your hands or forearms to the mat in Wide-Legged Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang as you breathe here, then slowly roll up.

Sit on the mat and straighten your legs in front of you, about hip-width apart. Slowly fold forward, resting your hands on your thighs, shins, or on the mat on either side of your legs in Seated Forward Fold. Relax your neck and let your head hang. Breathe here, then slowly roll up.

Come to your hands and knees. Walk your hands forward and slowly lower your forehead until it’s resting on the mat or a block in Melting Heart or Puppy Pose. Breathe here.

From Melting Heart, come to your hands and knees. Separate your knees and lower your hips toward your heels. Walk your hands between your legs and toward the wall behind you as you lower your shoulders onto the mat. Turn your head toward one side so one cheek is resting on the mat in a Child’s Pose variation. Breathe here.

After you come out of Child’s Pose, continue with your own version of a nighttime routine, eventually making your way to bed.

#8817. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images)

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

But I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

My doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I said.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A big reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my big question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

There’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, says David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

“When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”

In another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he said.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, says it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

“When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he says. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”

Instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor said my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment quickly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

But as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

What I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

He reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he said gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”

His advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, says Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

And, Moffat says, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she says. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”

In fact, she says, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

As for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

Self-care might be a personal undertaking, but that doesn’t mean you can’t give your people tools they’ll find useful along the way. This smart ring supports anyone who is so over any sort of tracking technology. If your giftee’s goal is less about personal optimization and more about simple reminders to enjoy life, Pulse is worth slipping on.

Any tool that helps the body feel relieved, relaxed, and de-puffed is a gift we can get behind. Sliding this oversized gua sha tool over lotioned or oiled limbs is one of my favorite self-care moments. Lymphatic drainage is an actual thing, but even if all that this giant gua sha is doing is giving me a good old-fashioned massage, I offer it my gratitude. If you or someone you know enjoys a multi-step evening routine, add this to the holiday list.

Yes, you can give the gift of a regulated nervous system. The Open app is a wonderland of breathwork, meditation, mindfulness, even yoga and movement classes. It’s also really, really pretty, which let’s be honest, is an important aspect of an app that’s designed to calm you down. I’ve admittedly fallen off my streak, but for a few months I was meditating daily (and happily) with Open. An Open credit pack allows you to gift that to someone else. Basically, for the person who wants to elevate their mindfulness routine but isn’t sure where to start, there’s an app for that.

I hold a lot of tension in my shoulders; I also work at a laptop all day everyday, which might have something to do with my tightness and pain. At the end of a massage a few years ago, the masseur very seriously told me to invest in a Theragun to help loosen some of my long-held knots. The mini version of the tool is lightweight and easy to grip, making at-home massage sessions simple. For what it’s worth, my shoulders have definitely loosened up.

Sitting in stillness, tuning in to your breath, and letting your thoughts float by is the work of a lifetime—and notoriously difficult. If a regular yoga practice aims to limber up your body so you can sit for longer stretches, a good set of meditation pillows can help make the prospect even more comfortable. This pretty, eco-friendly cushion makes meditation all the more aspirational. Who knows? This could be the start of your giftee’s mindfulness journey, or the thing that helps the sometimes-meditator develop a more consistent sitting session.

Cards such as “Cusp,” “Fifth House,” “The Moon,” and “Solar Eclipse” speak to life experience and celestial events, a welcome reminder of the interconnectedness of it all. Whether your loved one is a deck collector or just getting into their spiritual card game, they’ll appreciate learning something new (or cementing their astrological knowledge) on the daily. Plus, the psychedelic illustrations are enough to compel your giftee to pick a card, any card.

Comfortable enough to lounge in and capable enough for your daily workouts, this legging is buttery soft, breathable, and perfect for anyone on your holiday list with multiple color options to suit any style and fit.

A new journal is a fresh start. So, why not invest in a journal that’s been raved about by social media (particularly the JournalTok community, which is very much a thing)? This journal comes with a generous page count, allowing it to be whatever your loved one needs it to be—and challenging new owners to actually fill its 411 pages rather than getting a shiny, new notebook every few months. And for the organizational freaks among us, the notebook’s table of contents and numbered pages make it easier to actually keep track of your thoughts.

We are all obsessed with our smartphones. But if there’s a particular person in your life who could use a little extra help curbing their tech use, Brick is a solid gift. Is this entirely due to this therapy bag? Probably not. But if there’s a lover of wellness and innovation in your life, I guarantee they will appreciate taking in this at-home, full-body red light at their leisure.

#8814. 4 Winter Running Habits to Keep Building Endurance in the Off-Season—No Treadmill Required

Expert-backed ways to maintain your aerobic fitness when cold weather tests your routine.

When days get shorter, temperatures get colder, and you no longer have a race on the horizon, the motivation to run consistently can seriously start to wane.

But prioritizing your aerobic fitness all year means you don’t have to start from scratch when it comes time to train for a race again, says Brant Stachel, an Ontario-based USATF-certified endurance coach at Fast and Free Performance Coaching. “Anytime you’re taking big swaths of time off, you have to go back into rebuilding mode where you spend weeks getting back up to the fitness that you previously had,” he says.

Whether you’re a longtime treadmill hater in need of more exciting options or you simply don’t have access to one, we tapped experts for their best alternatives that allow you to maintain your endurance without hopping on the belt. Follow these habits to keep your aerobic engine revved in the off-season.

The minimum amount of training you need to do depends on your fitness level and your current (or most recent) training load. “If you’re somebody who’s running five to seven days a week, you probably still want to do three to four days a week,” Stachel suggests.

Even one to two days a week can keep you from starting completely from scratch in the spring season, says Danielle Kroot, DPT, certified run coach and physical therapist based in Portland, Maine. “It’s also keeping your tissues and muscles exposed to that type of load so that there’s not this shock to your system when you start training for a race again, and can help decrease injury risk,” she adds.

Keep in mind it usually takes six weeks of consecutive low-mileage weeks to really lose fitness gains, says Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach, so taking a few weeks off (especially if you’re recovering from marathon season) won’t do any harm; it’ll actually help you recharge.

Unless you’re training for marathons year-round, you’re likely periodizing your training, Stachel says, which means cycling through off-seasons, shorter distances, and maintenance mode in between major race training cycles. He explains that periodizing your training is really important for staying well-rounded and building adequate speed, strength, and endurance—all factors that make you a stronger, faster runner.

Winter is a great time to analyze any gaps or weaknesses in your fitness, especially following a fall marathon season, Stachel says. Look at your recent training cycles and factor in what didn’t work for you. You might address strength and injury prevention after dealing with nagging calf pain, or consider focusing on speed workouts you didn’t get to hit as much during a marathon season, like mile race pace, 3K, and 5K pace efforts, he adds.

Strength work builds stability, power, and durability for better performance, and can help you handle mileage and speed. Building more strength in the off-season will translate to more speed, power, and injury prevention when you decide to ramp mileage back up.

Off-season strength should generally target major muscle groups runners rely on most, like the calves, glutes, and quads. Both Dell and Kroot recommend focusing on deadlift variations, squat variations, lunges, calf raises, step-ups, and plyometric movements.

Generally, you want to choose weights that make you feel like you could do only two more repetitions; that signals that the weight is heavy enough, Kroot explains.

“Even if you’ve got those five-pound weights hanging out in your basement, you can see how many squats you can do until you feel close to exhaustion,” Stachel adds.

If you have limited equipment at home, each expert recommends combining movements, such as doing a 15-minute stair climb, followed by bodyweight burpees or planks.

One particularly snowy winter, Stachel broke up his 90-minute run into five different sections, utilizing the equipment at his local gym and combining running and cross-training in one session. He ran 15 minutes to his local gym, went on the elliptical for 20 minutes, biked for 20 minutes, went on the treadmill for 20 minutes, then ran 15 minutes home. “The idea of simply going on a treadmill for 90 minutes was mentally numbing,” he says.

Stachel explains that while it’s best to complete a 90-minute run through running alone to stay specific to your sport, you have to find a workout you can stick with. “The best winter workout is the one you’ll actually repeat and build on next week,” he says.

In the off-season, cross-training is your friend, Stachel says. Even if you don’t have any injuries, it’s a good idea to add some form of alternative aerobic-focused movement to your routine such as swimming, aqua jogging, elliptical, or cycling. “Then it doesn’t seem like a shock to the system when that first snowfall drops and you’ve got a week where you can’t go outside and run,” he adds. Stachel explains that gym memberships can be especially helpful for this reason.

Stachel’s go-to workout: a tempo session on the elliptical. “This has the closest carryover to running in terms of cardiovascular function,” he says. “It also loads the tissues because you’re more upright, whereas on the bike you don’t get that.”

You can do any run interval workout on the elliptical or another cross-training machine, Stachel says, but the general rule is to take your typical outdoor recovery time and cut it in half. For example, if you give yourself two minutes to recover between tempo intervals outside, take one-minute recoveries on the elliptical. This might look like three 10-minute bouts at tempo pace with one minute of easy efforts in between.

If you don’t typically go to a gym, Dell and Kroot recommend stair workouts, at-home workout videos that provide follow-along Zumba or high-intensity interval workouts, and jumping rope.

Each expert recommends making an effort to still get outside as much as possible, even if it’s once or twice a week, or more during weeks when your local weather cooperates. Bundling up for the occasional outdoor run keeps training exciting, and helps your body stay adjusted to the roads.

Here are a few of their tips for making the most of those outdoor runs.

Oftentimes the best way to stay consistent with running in the off-season is to find safe, paved places to run when roads might be wet or covered in snow. Stachel recommends asking other runners in your community or talking to runners at your local run store to find the best routes in your area.

“Every city I’ve been to or coached in during the winter has had some hidden gem that’s plowed for some reason,” Stachel says. This might be a municipal building, a local mall, hospital, or other parking lots. “Those little tips and tricks can make it all the more fun,” he adds.

Good gear becomes your armor for bracing cold winter runs. “If you’re out there and you’re underdressed, you’re miserable the entire time. If you’re overdressed, then you’re sweating through your clothes and your heart rate’s high and then you’re frustrated,” Dell says.

To dress according to winter weather, use the Runner’s World what to wear tool, which shows you how to layer based on different weather patterns. Dell also recommends investing in a good pair of fleece-lined tights or joggers, as well as ear covers and gloves. Stachel also recommends microspikes that you can strap onto running shoes for better traction on wet or snowy surfaces.

View the off-season as an opportunity to rise to another challenge, Stachel says. “There are so many times that as athletes, we feel hardcore for doing things. You could probably figure out a way to feel really hardcore for navigating a crazy winter or running,” he says, noting that a sense of empowerment comes from training through a season that many people don’t train through.

“Winter doesn’t change what builds endurance, it just changes how you collect it,” says Stachel. You might spend more time hacking your training and moving workouts indoors, or bundling up to run outside.

By spring, you can expect an “epic” racing season that feels rewarding and full of satisfaction because of all the hard work you put in during winter months, Stachel notes. Then, you will likely find the urge to continue training every winter because you know you’ll feel rewarded when the spring comes and you’re much closer to hitting your paces and PRs.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Promo Rewards typically drop in the first week of each month. Set a recurring reminder to check the FlyingBlue.com Promo Rewards page. Consistency is the single biggest factor in landing these deals.

Maintain balances in Chase UR, Amex MR, Citi ThankYou, or Capital One. When a promo appears, you need to transfer and book quickly. Having points spread across programs gives you flexibility and instant transfer capability.

When the monthly promo drops, scan the route list for your target destinations. If your preferred city is not on promotion, check connecting cities. A promo flight to Paris or Amsterdam plus a cheap intra-Europe connection can still deliver outstanding value.

Picture this: you settle into a fully flat bed at 35,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, the city lights of New York fading behind you. In seven hours, you'll be in Paris. But right now, in this seat — a seat that costs upward of $6,000 in cash — you paid 53,000 points to be here. That's the Air France Business Class experience on the JFK–CDG route, and it's one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions available to the ChooseFI community today. Let's talk about the math, because the math is what makes this a genuine FI moment. A round-trip business class ticket between New York and Paris on Air France routinely retails for $3,000 on the low end and climbs to $6,000 or beyond during peak travel periods. At 53,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, you're looking at a value of **5.7 to 11.3 cents per point** — in a world where most points are considered excellent at 1.5 to 2 cents. You are, quite literally, squeezing 3 to 7 times the average value out of every mile you've earned. The pricing inefficiency here is real and it's structural. Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program releases discounted award seats monthly, sometimes cutting standard pricing by 25–50%. When a Promo Reward surfaces on a transatlantic business class route, the gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you pay in miles becomes almost absurd. A $4,000 cash ticket redeemable for 53,000 points you transferred at no cost from your Chase Sapphire Reserve? That's **7.5 cents per point** — money that your future self will thank you for. Beyond the numbers is the *experience* itself. Air France's long-haul business class product on the Boeing 777-300ER features a fully flat bed in a 1-2-1 configuration, direct aisle access from every seat, genuine French hospitality, and a meal service that feels like a restaurant, not an afterthought. This isn't a product you suffer through — it's one you savor. For a community that builds wealth intentionally so they can live fully, this is exactly what travel rewards are designed to unlock: a world-class experience at a fraction of the cost, because you understood the system.

Monthly promotional pricing makes premium European travel consistently accessible

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

The Booking: You're flying JFK → CDG in Air France Business Class on a Boeing 777-300ER. It's a Tuesday evening departure — one of the best days for award availability — and you've snagged a Promo Reward seat at 53,000 Flying Blue miles plus approximately $65 in government taxes.

The Cash Alternative: A quick search on Google Flights shows the same seat retailing for $4,200 on that date. You earned them on purchases you were already making, transferred them in minutes, and unlocked a $4,200 experience for $65 out of pocket. That's the ChooseFI travel rewards system working exactly as designed.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

#8812. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

Keep your back health on track with these tips from top docs and bike-fit experts.

Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he says.

Herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” says bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

Your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” says Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”

You may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie says. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research shows that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, says Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very important when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier says. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:

Press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

Cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent says. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent says.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, says Broadbent.

Having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt says. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

An anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “big three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

McGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section)

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

Finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie says. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a big difference in your back health.”

And to think his whole running obsession started with what was supposed to be a simple walk.

In an October interview with Hypebeast, Khalifa explained that he’d gone out to a trail one day, decided to pick up the pace, and eventually checked his watch to discover he’d gone four miles. And to his surprise, he also realized he’d accidentally discovered a new hobby.

"Oh sh*t! I kind of liked that," he recalled.

Apparently, that was enough to get him investing in proper shoes and gear, and by July, he was documenting his workouts on social media, telling his Instagram followers how much he enjoyed getting out there with increasingly ambitious mileage goals (and even catching Strava's attention when the platform offered to help verify his account). More recently, he challenged himself to cover 30 miles in a week, telling fans, "You can join in or watch me be great."

Of course, given Khalifa's well-documented relationship with marijuana, there's an obvious question about how all this cardio is treating him. He certainly doesn't seem too concerned.

"My lungs are holding up great. I'm getting faster," he told Hypebeast, crediting his years of Muay Thai training and performing onstage for his endurance.

Whatever his routine, Khalifa certainly had plenty of energy left after Sunday's 5K. In a post-race Instagram video, he's seen enjoying every second of his new racing career, bouncing around, dancing, and proudly showing off his Strava results.

And as for his post-race celebration? He wound up in Diplo's DJ booth, of course.

#8810. The Best Heart Rate Monitors Give You the Most Accurate Training Data

We tested the best heart rate monitors so you can focus on the miles, not the math.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Tracking your heart rate with a heart rate monitor (HRM) during your runs is one of the most powerful ways to optimize your training, whether you’re a dedicated marathoner, power triathlete, or just aiming to move more intentionally. As a runner, I understand that my heart rate is important, but I don’t necessarily understand using it as a training device. That’s why I reached out to an expert to find out why it’s important and how to use that data.

As exercise physiologist and run coach Alyssa Lombardi tells Runner’s World, “Monitoring your heart rate while training can be a great tool to help you understand how hard your body is working. It’s important for a balanced training program to have lots of easy recovery days where your heart rate is low, balanced by some harder intensity workouts where your heart rate is high.” Understanding and utilizing heart-rate zones—ranging from zone 1 (very light) to zone 5 (maximum effort)—can help you tailor your training for performance, endurance, and recovery.

While zone 2 running gets loads of buzz as the golden ticket for endurance building and recovery, Lombardi emphasizes that “all zones have their place in a training program.” She also notes an important caveat: “As an exercise physiologist I can understand the benefits of heart rate training but when I am coaching my athletes I do not have them follow heart rate based training to a T because your heart rate can vary so much day to day.” Lombardi lists how factors like heat, hydration, location, and medications can change your heart rate. “It is a great tool to have but I never have my athletes follow that 100 percent.”

This nuanced approach is critical—HRMs are invaluable tools, but their data should be viewed in context. Each athlete responds differently, and some exceptionally fit runners may see higher heart rates at lower intensity simply because their bodies have adapted to efficiently sustain greater workloads.

As a side note, these are largely HSA/FSA eligible, so you might not be out-of-pocket for the cost. Just check your eligibility, and keep those receipts.

Alyssa Lombardi is a certified personal trainer, run coach, and clinical exercise physiologist with more than six years of experience. A former collegiate runner with a master’s in exercise science, she coaches athletes of all levels through her business, Run Fit With Me. Lombardi emphasizes individualized training, injury prevention, and strength work, blending evidence-based science with real-world experience to help runners get faster, stay healthy, and achieve their goals.

The Polar H10 stands out as the best overall heart rate monitor for its unmatched accuracy and comfort. Its ECG technology delivers precise data, making it a favorite among serious athletes. The soft, non-slip strap comes in multiple sizes, but women should note it can be a tricky fit with some supportive sports bras—though it works comfortably under lower-line running tank bras. Men with chest hair have mentioned a slight pulling sensation, but most find it secure once adjusted. With long battery life, waterproofing up to 30 meters, dual Bluetooth connectivity, and onboard memory, it’s a reliable companion for any training style.

The Powr Labs Chest Heart Rate Monitor offers solid performance for a fraction of the price of premium brands, making it a great budget-friendly option. I found the strap to be comfortable and adjustable, though the sensor is a bit bulky. Its dual ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity worked seamlessly with my Garmin and smartphone apps.

While it’s water-resistant, I’d avoid prolonged swimming sessions. It tracks heart rate reliably across different workouts, from running to CrossFit. The strap fits well on me, but it might feel a bit tight or loose for some depending on body shape. Overall, it’s a dependable, no-frills monitor that gets the job done without breaking the bank, especially if this is your first foray into HR training.

If you have a Forerunner 570 or above, you’ll know that some of the more advanced metrics like cadence and step speed loss require a heart rate monitor for measurement. This HRM is not only the best for that application but also one of the best we tested—period. It’s unbelievably comfy, it’s incredibly accurate, and it syncs seamlessly with whatever Garmin watch you use, and it’s not limited to only Garmin devices. You love your Apple Watch? Fab. Use it. You don’t run with a watch? First of all, how dare you. Second of all, it still works. You just need to link it to your phone instead. (You’re a rebel. I don’t get it, but I appreciate it.)

I do wish that it came in more and extended sizes. And honestly, if you’re stacked through the lats and pecs, it might not work, which is unfortunately pretty much true for the majority of chest straps. But for the majority of runners, this is an economical, comfortable, feature-packed choice that gets you into Garmin’s system. Welcome to the cult.

The Coros Heart Rate Monitor is my favorite pick when I want accurate tracking without the chest strap drama. The soft, stretchy fabric band hugs my upper arm comfortably—no digging, no slipping—and works well for a wide range of arm sizes. I barely feel it on long runs, and it never tangles with my tops. The optical sensor stays steady most of the time, though it can lag a bit on sudden sprints. It’s a bit more laggy than other HRMs I tested, by a few seconds. This is not a unique problem to Coros, but it is more noticeable here.

Battery life is solid at up to 38 hours, and Bluetooth syncing is quick, but the connection range isn’t amazing—you’ll want to keep your watch or phone fairly close. I’ve also noticed it can get a little itchy once I start sweating hard, so a quick postrun rinse is a must. Still, for comfort, simplicity, and ditching the chest strap, it’s a win in my book.

The Whoop Peak is a heckuva fun wearable device for deep health and fitness insights—tracking not just your heart rate, but also recovery, sleep quality, strain, and more. I love how all that data comes together to show me exactly when to push harder and when to rest. I am notorious for doing all the things, all at once, like training for a marathon while also working on a deadline for my book and keeping my demanding day job. This is great for my AuDHD brain, but can be hard on my body. The Whoop dials into that and lets me know I’ve been going too hard and my recovery metrics are showing that. The only real trade-off with this wearable? You have to look at your phone for every stat, since the band has no face or display.

And while you do pay for a monthly membership to access the full suite of features, the first year is included, which makes it easier to justify. It doesn’t warn you as often as the Oura ring or a Garmin device about your habits, but features a lighter touch in the “you’re overdoing it” shame department.

The Garmin HRM-Fit has totally changed how I think about heart rate straps. Instead of wrapping around my chest like the usual band (and fighting with my sports bra every run), it clips right onto the underband of a medium- or high-support bra. No chafing, no slipping—just accurate tracking that feels almost invisible once I get going.

It did take a minute to learn how to get the clips sitting just right, but now it’s second nature. My heart rate data is spot-on, and I love that it pairs instantly with my Garmin watch and other devices via Bluetooth or ANT+. The chunky clips do show under tight tops, so it’s not exactly stealthy, but the yearlong battery life makes up for it. For me, it’s comfort, accuracy, and freedom—all in one.

I am a big fan of the upgrades on the Oura Ring 5. First of all, it’s a lot slimmer and lighter than previous models, and it also doesn’t scratch as easily. On top of that, the battery life is much improved. But what really matters is what the ring does.

It’s an accurate HRM that picks up activities easily, sometimes too easily, as it can occasionally register things like vacuuming as “dancing” or cleaning the bathroom as “HIIT.” Though that might speak more to the vigor with which I scrub the bathroom than any mistake of the ring itself.

When I’m on my run, it tracks my heart rate, oxygen, and effort and gives me insights on where I can improve and what I can do to achieve that, and it’s easy to understand and well thought out. But what I really love is how it looks at my cycle, and helps me understand how that might be affecting my workouts. As it turns out, perimenopause is messing with my life hard-core, and now my previously unpredictable cycle has become even more unpredictable, and it’s making my runs around my period so much worse.

But there’s help in the app for that, as well. In the app, you can connect with health practitioners or link to your own healthcare provider, upload your labs, food diary, and more, and get advice based on your current goals and situation. I recently linked to my primary care doctor and my hematologist to determine just how my cycle, training, diet, and anemia were affecting each other, and we came up with a plan for treatment. To the infusion clinic I go! Before I had this ability, the process was a lot longer and a much bigger pain in the butt. Now, my doctors and I can make concrete plans far more easily, and it’s been a big blessing.

Accuracy is paramount for heart rate monitors. A reliable HRM provides consistent, precise heart rate readings during various activities, from cardio to strength training. Inaccurate readings can undermine workout effectiveness and hinder fitness progress, making you wonder if your heart is even trying.

When it comes to heart rate tracking, it’s all about what feels right for you, especially when you’re really pushing it. Chest straps give you accurate readings but can be a bit annoying, while wrist monitors and rings are convenient but might glitch out during intense workouts. So, the real MVP here is whatever you’ll actually wear and trust for your grind—try ’em both if you can.

Say goodbye to connection woes. Thanks to Bluetooth and ANT+, gadgets play nice with all your beloved external devices and go-to fitness apps. Some even have the ability to send the readings right to your doctor.

No one likes a dead heart rate monitor in the middle of a workout, so think about how often you’ll need to swap out those batteries. Make sure you have a good stash of fresh ones on hand, or consider rechargeable options to keep the fun going. That way, your entertainment won’t be interrupted by a sudden power outage.

A durable HRM needs to keep up with your lifestyle, whether you’re breaking a sweat or just enjoying a brisk walk. Chest bands are generally very durable, while smartwatches and wristbands offer good longevity but may be a bit more precious, and smart health tracking rings are designed for continuous wear and can withstand daily activities but may scratch.

Running dynamics, on-device memory, and water resistance can enhance utility for diverse athletes. Additionally, some advanced watches and rings offer features like period and ovulation prediction, providing valuable health insights for users. These capabilities make them more than just fitness trackers, transforming them into comprehensive personal health companions.

These can get pricey. Select a monitor that fits your budget and needs, and don’t forget that some, like the Whoop and Oura ring, have additional membership fees.

Many standard heart rate monitors—especially chest straps and armbands—pose real and annoying challenges for size inclusivity. Limited strap size ranges often make them too small for bigger runners and too large or bulky for petite athletes, affecting comfort, fit, and even accuracy.

For women with large breasts who require more supportive bras, chest straps can be particularly tricky. Supportive or high-compression bras may push the strap down, create pressure points, or cause shifting, which can lead to discomfort, chafing, or inconsistent readings. When shopping for a heart rate monitor, it’s important to consider not only strap length and adjustability but also how well the design works with your body type and workout apparel to ensure both comfort and reliable data.

How accurate are wrist-based HRMs compared to chest straps?Wrist-based optical sensors are good these days—accurate enough for most people—but chest straps still win during activities with sudden heart rate spikes or lots of wrist movement.

Do I need a subscription for my HRM?Most HRMs don’t require one, but some, like Whoop or Oura, do charge a monthly membership for access to their full analytics and insights. That subscription cost is worth factoring into your budget.

Can heart rate monitors detect health issues?HRMs aren’t medical devices, but trends in your heart rate, recovery, or heart rhythm can signal changes worth discussing with your healthcare provider. Some devices, like the Apple Watch, even have FDA-cleared ECG apps to record heart rhythm data.

#8808. Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family)

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:

1. Procrastination is Expensive — Swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes

27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

29. There Are Steps — Once you have finished your first sprint triathlon, take the following actions (in order): a) Sign up for an Ironman, b) Sign up for a Hyrox, c) Advertise your coaching services.

30. Triathlon = Procrastination (Always) — Finally, swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

#8807. How Yoga Supported Me Through Cancer (In Ways That Had Nothing to Do With Movement)

“You’ll need surgery,” my doctor said. “After that, no yoga.”

Moments before, she had informed me that I had endometrial cancer, and it felt as if an anvil had landed on my chest. My mind flooded with questions I couldn’t yet articulate. Somewhere in that static, I tried to recall exactly what she said about the diagnosis. And wait, no yoga?

Yoga was the practice I turned to whenever life got big. And this was huge. As my doctor explained the “good news” was that we caught the cancer early, and if all went well I wouldn’t need chemo, I tried to focus. She said I’d likely need a full hysterectomy, followed by months of recovery with limited movement. My heart sunk. How was I supposed to navigate cancer without the thing that always helped me navigate all the other things?

I immediately stepped into a new rhythm, my calendar filling with appointments for testing, bloodwork, and specialists. I wrote down hospital addresses and watched as needle after needle entered my veins. I freaked out as bills racked up and I had to repeatedly check in with my insurance company because things were insanely complicated. I tried to let go of control where I could and take charge where I needed. It was exhausting.

At each appointment, I had to tell the cancer story all over again. As I traveled around New York City, I secretly hoped I’d find someone who would tell me this was all a mistake. It felt like my body had betrayed me or that I was suddenly in skin that wasn’t my own.

Most of the time I left a doctor’s office and went straight to a yoga class. I needed to feel my feet underneath me, to soothe my mind and heart with deep breaths. I told myself I was going to practice yoga as much as I could in the months leading up to surgery, almost as if I could stockpile it in my bones. It was often the only time I felt at home in my body.

Yoga provided a hum of consistency. There, on the mat, I felt that familiar alchemy of turning my anxieties over to the practice. I breathed. I moved. During these months of consultations and biopsies and test results, yoga was the only time I felt okay, sometimes even good, in my body.

Yet sometimes in Down Dog, it felt like my entire heart turned into a teardrop, heavy with emotion. I cried in Child’s Pose, processing the layers of emotions associated not just with the cancer but the fact that I’d be losing a part of my body.

Other times, I was hit with denial, fear, and shock. How had this happened? I was only in my 40s, and the most common age range for endometrial cancer was the 60s. Sometimes, lying in Corpse Pose, I’d let myself think about the truth underlying cancer, feeling my mortality. I was staring impermanence in the face.

Yoga was a place to feel all the things. Yet more often than not, I ended practice feeling awash with a rare calm I no longer took for granted. I wished I could escape into the post-yoga glow forever. I was clinging! Still, I wished there was a way.

The day of my surgery finally came, and it was time to say goodbye to my cancer, my uterus, and, at least for a while, yoga.

That morning, sitting in my hospital gown on a gurney waiting to enter the OR, I tried to stay centered, but my body took over. I broke out in a cold sweat. Nausea rolled through me and my breath caught in my chest. The room swirled.

“You’re having a panic attack,” my doctor said, placing her hand on my back. I inhaled and exhaled for a count of five, over and over, instinctively practicing box breathing while trying not to jostle the many tubes hooked to me. My body knew this language. It eventually began to calm down.

In the days after surgery, my pelvis blared with pain. I couldn’t even sit up on my own in bed without wanting to pass out. Lying motionless and still feeling discomfort, I began to understand what the doctor had meant by taking a break from the poses. I couldn’t just unroll my mat and fall into Child’s Pose.

But I was starting to sense the ways yoga was still with me, even approaching me in this moment of pain and need.

While stuck in bed, I thought of the yoga teaching of purusha and prakriti. Purusha is the witness self, the spirit, the part of us that watches our experiences. Prakriti is the material world, including the body. As I cared for myself, taking my medications on a complicated rotation and hobbling around throughout the day to avoid blood clots, I realized I could watch my body yet also dwell in a different part of myself. I felt a small space between my body self and my witness self, and this space felt like a lifesaver.

Propped up by pillows, I listened to a recording of a yoga nidra guided meditation. The voice brought my awareness to various parts of my body that I hadn’t contemplated in months. One of my teachers, Dharma Mittra, had described yoga nidra as closing the open tabs on your computer, or your thoughts, while keeping the computer, or your consciousness, on.

Now I closed down one thing at a time, mentally minimizing the cancer, the pain, even the act of healing, and felt into the parts of me beyond that. I breathed and observed.

I felt inside me a quiet resilience I’d spent years getting to know and grow on the mat. I was in a forced state of slowing down, and here I saw a glimmer of an unprecedented intimacy with my life that no Netflix binge would blot out.

As I began to move through healing, I realized even pursuing treatment had been ahimsa, or non-violence practice, toward myself. I began to understand that my body hadn’t betrayed me. It was still my friend, just someone going through something, and my practice had been to try to be kind to it, advocate on my own behalf.

Coming to terms with cancer and the impermanence of my body had been a kind of satya, or honesty, practice. Walking the healing path and heading into surgery had been a sort of act of surrender, ishvara pranidana. Somewhere along the way I’d released into a kind of trust and faith that I would be carried by a higher power.

I realized there was so much of the yoga practice already deeply within me beyond the poses. It was a relief: yoga wasn’t going anywhere. Neither was I. The practice’s philosophy and lessons were an invisible scaffolding supporting all aspects of my life.  I even felt a sense of joy remembering I was more than my body.

Yoga was strengthening me just when I most needed it. It was teaching me about myself, a kind of svadhyaya, or self-study.

Yoga didn’t “save” me. It didn’t distract me from the realities of my situation. What it did was provide me with tools and a framework for navigating those realities and remaining acutely present with myself throughout the better part of a year. I had built these tools over decades of practice, and they were indeed inside me, deeper than I even knew.

I’d given myself to yoga years earlier. Now, it was giving back to me.

A few months after my surgery, I went to yet another post-op appointment. I was tired of being poked and prodded, but as my doctor checked my stitches, I stepped into the role of witness again, more consciously this time.

“You’re cancer-free!” she said, reviewing the final pathology report. “You’re now a cancer survivor. You can go back to yoga now.”

I didn’t tell her, but I’d been practicing all along.
